meta.name: Jess Cole
meta.description: Writer and teacher in Boston — fiction, poetry, essays, and writing workshops
meta.author: EmDash

children.text: Jess Cole is a writer and teacher living in Boston with her son. Her work — fiction, poetry, and essays — keeps circling the same two questions: what a place does to the people who live in it, and what those people carry with them when they leave.

She studied International Relations and French at Boston University, earned an M.A. in English at UC Davis, and wrote a novel as her doctoral dissertation at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. Along the way she has published articles, book chapters, short fiction, and Pushcart-nominated poems.
Teaching

Jess has taught college writing for years, including as writer-in-residence and visiting professor at the University of Graz in Austria and at the ProArts colleges in Boston. She now teaches small generative workshops — essays, fiction, and the stories of place — and works as a book coach at Bloomsday Literary, helping writers carry a manuscript from first draft to finished book.
If you're curious about a class or want help with a manuscript, get in touch — she reads everything.

data.title: The Personal Essay
data.summary: A generative afternoon on the essay — finding the true subject under the one you thought you were writing about. All levels welcome.

$media.alt: An open notebook with handwritten pages and a pen

children.text: Every essay has two subjects: the thing it's about, and the thing it's really about. In this three-hour workshop we read a few short essays that make that gap visible, then write into our own material with timed prompts. You'll leave with two rough starts and a way of asking your drafts what they're actually up to.
What to bring
A notebook and something to write with — or a laptop, if that's how you draft. No prior workshop experience needed, and nothing has to be shared aloud unless you want to.

data.title: Writing Place
data.summary: A workshop on setting as more than backdrop — how a street, a kitchen, or a whole city can carry a story's meaning.

$media.alt: An open book and coffee on a wooden table by a window

children.text: Place is where fiction and memory keep their evidence. We'll look at how writers make a setting do real work — carrying class, history, and longing without announcing any of it — and then write from places you know well enough to be honest about. Expect close reading, timed generative writing, and gentle feedback in pairs.
Who it's for
Anyone writing fiction or nonfiction where the where matters — which is nearly everyone. The class is capped at ten so there's time for every voice.

data.title: Short Fiction: First Drafts
data.summary: An evening for getting a story started — momentum over polish, with prompts designed to outrun your inner editor.

$media.alt: A desk with notebooks, books, and a warm lamp

children.text: First drafts die of self-consciousness more often than lack of talent. This evening session is built for momentum: a short craft talk on openings, then three rounds of timed writing from prompts that give you a character, a place, and a problem before your inner editor wakes up. You'll leave with the raw material of at least one story.

data.title: Short Fiction
data.summary: Published short stories about people caught between the places that made them and the places they've landed.

$media.alt: A vintage typewriter with a page mid-sentence

children.text: The stories tend to start with a place — a rented kitchen in Graz, a triple-decker in Boston, a Tennessee highway at night — and follow the people who can't quite belong to it. Several have appeared in literary journals; more are always in the drawer, getting rewritten.
What they circle

Displacement, mostly — the ordinary kind. A character moves for school, for work, for someone else's dream, and the story watches what the new place asks them to give up. The endings are rarely tidy. The good ones weren't tidy in life either.

data.title: Poems
data.summary: Pushcart-nominated poems — compressed, image-driven, and rooted in specific rooms and streets.

$media.alt: An open book with pages fanned in soft light

children.text: The poems are where the compression happens — what takes a story twenty pages, a poem has to do in twenty lines. Two have been nominated for the Pushcart Prize. Most begin as field notes: something overheard on the Green Line, the particular light in a stairwell, a phrase in Austrian German that has no honest translation.
New work appears in journals now and then; a first collection is slowly assembling itself.

data.title: Essays & Chapters
data.summary: Published articles and book chapters — on writing, teaching, and the way language carries identity across borders.

$media.alt: A stack of well-read books on a table

children.text: The nonfiction runs alongside the creative work: articles and book chapters on writing pedagogy, on teaching college writing to students who arrive with more languages than confidence, and on what it means to write about a place as a guest in it — a question sharpened by two years teaching in Graz, Austria.
The essays are also where the teaching and the writing talk to each other — much of what ends up in the workshops started as a problem worked out on the page here.

data.title: The Novel
data.summary: A novel written as a doctoral dissertation — a long story about home, told from the far side of leaving it.

$media.alt: A dim library aisle lined with books

children.text: The novel was written as a doctoral dissertation at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville — a book-length answer to the question the shorter work keeps asking: whether you can ever really narrate the place you're from, or only the person it made.
Where it stands

The dissertation draft is done; the revision — the part where a defensible manuscript becomes a readable book — is ongoing, in the gaps between teaching and coaching other people's manuscripts at Bloomsday Literary. It is patient work, and the book is patient with her.
